alt: Three columns: post-2000 prose (Harvest, Brotherless Night, The Kite Runner), poetry (Blake’s Songs of Innocence and of Experience, pre-1900, or Tony Harrison’s Selected Poems), and a further text (Hard Times, A Doll’s House and Henry IV Part I, all pre-1900, or The Handmaid’s Tale). One of the three texts must be pre-1900, and A Doll’s House must be the Meyer translation.
caption: One post-2000 novel, one poetry text and one further text, with at least one pre-1900.

alt: AQA’s core idea, power and powerlessness central to each text, sits above six groups with examples: type of text, settings for power struggles, the nature of the struggle, the smaller world and the larger, gender and class, and structure and language. A note adds comment and audience.
caption: Six groups of elements, each illustrated from the set texts.

alt: Nested rings run from the domestic world through the workplace to society and government, each with an example: the politics of a marriage in A Doll’s House, a father’s working life as a question of class in Marked with D, and one child linked to a society’s cruelty in The Chimney Sweeper.
caption: Protest texts tie private and domestic power to the wider social order.

alt: Two columns analyse the original extract. Power: the rules called a kindness, verbless commands with no speaker, and payment in company-shop tokens. Resistance: the chalked words We are not looms, a handwritten voice against print, and three different hands. Below, Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday show the rules posted, the chalk scrubbed off and the chalk back, a cycle in which protest survives erasure.
caption: Power speaks through rules; resistance answers in a human voice that keeps returning.

alt: A balance tips towards the powerless: both texts centre on a woman in a system controlled by men and show power depending on the cooperation of the powerless. The counter-view notes the carefully drawn Torvald and Commander and Atwood’s Historical Notes. The judgement is that both examine power through the powerless but question who controls the story.
caption: Both texts look at power from below, then ask who controls the telling.
